overview: Picture a map with two Buyid shapes at once, and one of them is in the wrong neighborhood. The atlas id buyid-emirate exists only from 1000 to 1100, yet its polygon lies across coastal Balochistan and Sindh, far east of Baghdad, Ray and Shiraz. The separate buwayhid-emirates shape covers those real Buyid centers. History is clearer than the artwork: three Daylamite brothers built related principalities in the 930s, and Ahmad entered Baghdad in 945. The Abbasid caliph remained a revered religious leader, while Buyid amirs commanded armies and government. Their courts supported libraries, hospitals, astronomers, builders and busy trade ports. Their family confederation was never one tidy, permanently united empire; cousins and brothers competed, and local rulers gained ground. Seljuk forces ended Buyid control of Baghdad in 1055, while the last southern branch fell by about 1062. People did not vanish with the dynasty: farmers, merchants, scholars, craftspeople and city neighborhoods continued under new rulers.

periods.title: Three brothers build related principalities
periods.summary: Ali, Hasan and Ahmad ibn Buya rose from Daylamite military service and won territories in Fars, Jibal, Kerman and Khuzestan. Their conquests formed a family of regional governments, not a single state with fixed borders.

periods.title: Buyid power enters Baghdad
periods.summary: Ahmad entered Baghdad in December 945 and received the title Muizz al-Dawla. The Abbasid caliph stayed in place, while Buyid military rulers relied on local officials and controlled much of political life.

periods.title: Adud al-Dawla briefly joins the major branches
periods.summary: After family conflict, Adud al-Dawla controlled Fars, Iraq and wide neighboring territories. His short peak of power joined warfare and close administration with dams, markets, hospitals, libraries and new urban projects.

periods.title: Successors divide the confederation again
periods.summary: After Adud al-Dawla died, competing relatives fought over Fars and Iraq. Fars had prospered under him, but repeated conflict weakened revenue, security and cooperation among the related Buyid courts.

periods.title: A queen mother rules Ray as local powers rise
periods.summary: Sayyida governed the Ray principality for her young son from 997 to 1014. Meanwhile a Buyid-linked Kakuyid governor gained power at Isfahan, showing how nominal service could grow into practical independence.

periods.title: Northern losses and pressure on Iraq
periods.summary: Ghaznavid forces took Ray in 1029, and Seljuk armies later captured Isfahan. Buyid rule continued in Iraq and Fars, but separate branches could no longer build an effective common defense.

periods.title: Baghdad and Fars pass to new powers
periods.summary: Tughril Beg entered Baghdad in 1055 and imprisoned the last Buyid ruler there. A southern line remained in Fars until about 1062, when Shabankara conquest preceded Seljuk control.

sections.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass

items.text: The exact target is id “buyid-emirate,” labeled Buyid Emirate and indexed circa 1000 to 1100. Its only feature is one Polygon with one ring and 32 coordinate positions. Its decoded bounds run from about 63.600° to 71.405° east and 23.675° to 32.532° north.

No tested historical Buyid center falls inside the target polygon: Baghdad, Basra, Ahvaz, Shiraz, Siraf, Fasa, Isfahan, Hamadan, Ray and Kerman are all outside. Karachi, Hyderabad in Sindh, Thatta and Khuzdar are inside, exposing a severe placement error rather than a forgotten eastern Buyid capital.

A different feature called buwayhid-emirates appears in the same 1000 snapshot. Its two-part MultiPolygon contains every tested Buyid center from Baghdad to Kerman. Because the two geometries coexist and disagree, this card does not silently alias buyid-emirate to the separately carded Buwayhid record.

The target is absent in 900 and 1100. At 900 the atlas assigns many western test points to the Abbasid Caliphate; at 1100 it assigns the same region to the Seljuk Empire. These century snapshots are display layers, not exact conquest dates or proof of uniform control.

The identity problem gets stranger in 1200: buwayhid-emirates reappears over Iran and Iraq, while buyid-dynasty appears as a six-point polygon near Afghanistan and Pakistan. Both are centuries too late. The existing shared card remains separate; this target receives its own audited card and no appliesTo list.

sections.title: A family confederation, not one solid block

items.text: The founders were three sons of Buya from the mountainous Daylam region south of the Caspian. They first served other commanders, then seized different territories. Their shared family identity helped cooperation, but each brother built a regional court with its own soldiers, officials and ambitions.

Ray, Shiraz and Baghdad functioned as principal capitals, with Isfahan and other cities serving related courts. A messenger could not walk into one permanent Buyid capital and find every decision-maker there. Authority moved through a network of relatives whose rank and territory changed with inheritance and war.

When Ahmad entered Baghdad in 945, the Abbasid caliph did not disappear. The caliph retained religious prestige and granted titles, while the Buyid amir held military and political power. This layered arrangement explains why the names of both caliph and amirs could appear in public ritual and on coins.

After Fakhr al-Dawla died in 997, his widow Sayyida governed Ray for their four-year-old son. Her authority grew from a particular royal household and alliance network. It proves that one woman exercised sustained high power, not that women of every rank had the same choices.

Family ties could also sharpen conflict. Adud al-Dawla fought a cousin for Iraq, and later branches disputed seniority and provinces. The word dynasty can sound orderly, but succession meant negotiations, banquets, signed acknowledgments, rebellions and sometimes violence among people who were close relatives.

Buyid governments kept older administrative offices for finance, official correspondence and the army. Clerks still had to assess revenue, write orders and record military obligations. A new ruling family changed who commanded the system, but it did not erase every office or skill inherited from Abbasid government.

Many soldiers received an iqta, an assignment to collect revenue from land as pay. Under Buyid rules these grants were normally reassigned and did not automatically give the soldier legal authority over local residents. The army office estimated their fiscal value, turning fields and taxes into military accounts.

A Fasa silver dirham from 959 or 960 names the caliph al-Muti, Rukn al-Dawla and Adud al-Dawla. Three authorities fit on a coin only 25.7 millimeters wide and weighing 2.91 grams. Money carried a miniature chart of layered rule into markets and purses.

Court rank was performed as well as written. Thrones, audiences, titled amirs, viziers, commanders and attendants made hierarchy visible. Surviving court descriptions tell us far more about elite ceremony than about a porter’s workday, so this evidence should not be mistaken for everyone’s social life.

Buyid Baghdad depended on mixed expertise. Early rulers used Turkish soldiers, locally recruited bureaucrats and workers brought from Ahvaz and Isfahan for palace construction. Government was therefore not a single ethnic team; military households, scribes, builders and city communities met within one changing political system.

Excavated houses at Siraf often placed rooms around an open courtyard and used stairs to reach an upper story. Some windowless ground floors stored goods or may have been rented to poorer residents. Architecture hints at wealth differences, but it does not reveal every household’s kinship or sleeping arrangements.

Building space at Siraf was tight, so residents often repaired existing houses and adjusted facades to neighboring streets. Some homes were large and decorated; nearby shops could be only about three by two meters. A wealthy port still contained cramped work spaces and households with unequal resources.

Buyid rulers favored Shiite scholars, especially in Baghdad’s Karkh district, and a vizier founded a major library there in 991 or 992. Sunni institutions, the Abbasid caliph, Jewish communities and others continued. Patronage encouraged learning, while sectarian rivalry could also bring intimidation and violence.

Medieval Shiraz included Sunni Muslims, Shiite patrons, Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians, and residents also celebrated Iranian festivals. Labels at court cannot describe every neighbor’s practice. Religion shaped law, calendars, study and public ceremonies, but city life joined communities with different traditions and unequal political protection.

The evidence reviewed here does not provide a typical Buyid family size or a rule that every home followed. Royal genealogies show strategic marriages and inheritance; courtyard houses show shared domestic space; neither tells us exactly who cooked, cared for children or controlled money in an ordinary household.

sections.title: Food, markets and things that traveled

items.text: The province around Arrajan sent date and grape syrups, olive oil, soap and cloth into long-distance trade. Sources also list dates, nuts, olives, grapes, oranges and lemons. These products make a vivid regional pantry, though a trade list cannot reconstruct one child’s breakfast or every family’s diet.

British Museum records identify ninth- and tenth-century cooking pots made in India and excavated at Siraf. A sturdy kitchen vessel could cross the Indian Ocean before holding food in a Gulf port. The catalogue establishes origin, date and findspot, but not the cook, recipe or household that used it.

Siraf’s elegant houses stood beside a bazaar that survived for centuries, while ships connected the port with East Africa and the Far East. Merchants depended on sailors, pack animals, warehouse workers, brokers and craftspeople. Imported luxury was visible, but most of the labor behind it remains unnamed.

Excavation found small bazaar lockups, some with ovens, as well as imported raw material, metalworking and a pottery complex with thirty kilns. Markets were places of making as well as buying. Heat, smoke, tools, clay and repeated skilled motions filled workdays that court chronicles rarely describe.

A tenth-century gold ewer names the Buyid ruler Bakhtiyar, but its handle is probably later. A silk once labeled Buyid is now dated by the Met to the early twentieth century. Museum research can rewrite an object’s story, so neither luxury piece should become automatic evidence for ordinary Buyid tables or clothing.

sections.title: Water, baths and the toilet question

items.text: The Band-e Amir weir crossed the Kor River near Shiraz. Masonry foundations and stonework raised water for irrigation, while ten waterwheels reportedly lifted it toward hundreds of villages; the structure also carried a bridge. Royal funding mattered, but builders, farmers and repair crews made the system work.

Shiraz drew drinking water from mountain springs, and Rokn al-Dawla built a subterranean channel carrying spring water about ten kilometers to the city. Gardens produced fruits, flowers and vegetables. Water linked daily drinking, food growing, prestige and maintenance long before anyone could turn a tap.

At Siraf, earthenware pipes carried roof water into stone-lined pits, and excavators found stone-lined drains. Streets were unpaved, alleys could fill with rubbish, and even rich houses sometimes had weak sewage arrangements. Medieval sanitation was practical in places and seriously limited in others.

A public bath at Siraf, built before 1050, had an entry or changing room, an unheated room, warm rooms over hypocaust floors and a hot room heated by a furnace. It also included drains and a latrine. Bathing required fuel, water, engineering and staff, not just a pool.

The Great Mosque at Siraf gained rooms for ablution, latrines and storage during repeated rebuilding. That is direct toilet evidence for a public institution, not proof that every home had the same facilities. Archaeology gives us particular drains and rooms, while household habits remain unevenly visible.

Adud al-Dawla founded endowed hospitals, including a famous institution in Baghdad and another in Shiraz. One Shiraz complex taught medicine, astronomy, philosophy and mathematics. Hospitals were organized institutions with staff and funding, though the sources do not give a patient diary or survival rate.

Ibn Marzuban studied religious law and sciences and became superintendent of the Adudi hospital as well as a judge. His administrative role is clearer than his treatment of patients. The record reminds us that caring for the sick required budgets, supplies and supervision alongside medical knowledge.

The physician al-Majusi dedicated the Complete Book of the Medical Art to Adud al-Dawla. A surviving National Library of Medicine copy was made in 1208 by a Christian scribe, centuries after the dedication. It proves the work’s later transmission, not that this manuscript sat in a Buyid hospital.

Adud al-Dawla studied Arabic, geometry and astronomy, and his Shiraz library kept a separate list for each subject. That sounds almost like a catalog search before computers. It documents elite and specialist learning; it does not show that every child attended school or could read.

Abu Said al-Sirafi, born at the Gulf port, became a leading grammarian in Baghdad. His father came from a Zoroastrian family and converted to Islam. A scholar’s path could cross religion, language, port trade and capital-city teaching, but one famous career is not a literacy rate.

sections.title: Stars, art and words on metal and stone

items.text: Al-Sufi’s Book of the Fixed Stars combined inherited constellation knowledge with his own observations. It paired drawings with tables giving star coordinates calculated for 964. Readers could compare a picture in a book with measured positions overhead, and later astronomers continued to use the work.

A brass astrolabe signed by al-Khujandi in 984 or 985 has pointers for thirty-three stars; some end in little birds’ heads. The portable instrument could help tell time, find prayer direction and study the sky. Its signature survives, but its exact first owner does not.

Adud al-Dawla left a commemorative inscription at Persepolis in 955 or 956 that included Persian names in Arabic writing. Choosing an ancient royal site connected new power with an older landscape. The inscription records elite memory-making, not a return to the language or government of ancient Persia.

An authentic Buyid written sample is “الامير العدل” (al-amīr al-ʿadl), translated by the Ashmolean as “the Just Amir.” It appears in Arabic script on the reverse of Adud al-Dawla’s silver Fasa dirham from 959 or 960. This is coin titulature, not an ordinary person’s spoken sentence.

Putting a ruler’s name on a dirham announced political autonomy, while keeping the Abbasid caliph’s name signaled religious allegiance. The same coin could therefore speak in more than one political voice. Readers should treat its formula as an official message, not neutral reporting.

sections.title: How Buyid rule ended and what continued

items.text: In 1029 Ghaznavid Sultan Mahmud seized Ray, deposed Majd al-Dawla and ended the northern Buyid principality. A related Kakuyid ruler still maneuvered around Isfahan and Hamadan. Political change happened branch by branch, so one dramatic “fall of the empire” date would hide the real sequence.

Seljuk forces captured Isfahan in 1051 after a destructive siege. The city then recovered as people returned, taxes were suspended temporarily and buildings were repaired. A conquest could end one political arrangement while the streets, workshops and resident communities became part of another.

Tughril Beg entered Baghdad in 1055 and the last Buyid amir there was imprisoned. The Abbasid caliph remained, now under Seljuk power. The atlas’s clean 1100 Seljuk shape compresses this transition, but the political handoff in Baghdad has a specific historical date.

A Buyid branch survived in Fars until about 1062. Shabankara forces took the province before it passed under Seljuk control, so the structured successor link points to the atlas’s Seljuk id while the prose preserves the intermediate conquest. That distinction prevents a neat but false one-step story.

Dynasties end more quickly than daily systems. Buyid patrons disappeared, yet Arabic scholarship, hospitals, irrigation works, markets, coins, cultivated land and mixed city populations continued to change under Ghaznavid, Kakuyid, Shabankara and Seljuk rulers. Continuity belonged to people and places, not an atlas label.

ending.text: Buyid rule ended in stages rather than on the atlas boundary. Ghaznavids took Ray in 1029, Seljuks captured Isfahan in 1051 and Tughril Beg ended Buyid government in Baghdad in 1055. A southern line held Fars until about 1062, when Shabankara forces conquered it before Seljuk control followed. The successor link therefore points to the atlas’s Seljuk Empire id while preserving that intermediate step. Abbasid caliphs, city residents, farms, markets, hospitals, books, waterworks and craft traditions continued under new political masters. The eastern buyid-emirate polygon and the late 1200 Buyid labels are map errors, not surviving states.
